title: The Odyssey Episode
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with Jerry's banter in the intro) discuss Homer's Odyssey: its likely oral origins, 8th-century BCE writing, Ionic Greek, translation history (including George Chapman's 1616 English translation and Emily Wilson's 2017 version), the Homeric question, the themes of xenia (hospitality) and nostos (homecoming), a plot summary of the poem, the historical basis of Troy (Hisarlik), allegorical readings of monsters, the 2026 Christopher Nolan film adaptation and its cast, adaptations like Ulysses, The Penelopiad and O Brother, Where Art Thou?, and the lost sequel Telegony. Ends with a listener mail about rope and pulleys.

segments.title: Cold open banter
segments.summary: Playful opening banter about breastplates and codpieces leads into the hosts saying they will discuss the Odyssey, prompted by the Christopher Nolan film.

segments.title: Reactions to the Nolan Odyssey film
segments.summary: Josh shares his opinion of Christopher Nolan's films and says he liked the new Odyssey movie, noting how an ancient story still resonates in 2026.

segments.title: Origins of the Odyssey and Homer's attribution
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the Odyssey and Iliad are attributed to Homer, first written down around the 8th century BCE after a long oral tradition, and that the Odyssey is a sequel to the Iliad. Josh describes the 24 books and their coverage of Agamemnon's return and Odysseus's long journey home.

segments.title: Oral tradition and the written text
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the poem was passed down orally by bards, possibly changing like a game of telephone, until it was written on papyrus. It was central to Greek education, and Plato tried to ban it without success.

segments.title: Printing and early English translation
segments.summary: Josh outlines the poem's path to print: a first print copy in 1488 in Italy in Ionic Greek, European translations about a century later, and George Chapman's 1616 English translation.

segments.title: Meter and the challenges of translation
segments.summary: The hosts describe the dactylic hexameter the poem was composed in and why translators must make big choices. They compare translation difficulty to translating the Bible.

segments.title: Hard job of translating the Odyssey
segments.summary: Josh and the host note the difficulties of translating a dead language, an oral poem, and very old material, and omit a bawdy joke about a goat.

segments.title: Emily Wilson's 2017 translation
segments.summary: Emily Wilson's 2017 English translation in heroic couplets is named as the one most people are talking about now, and it is the one Christopher Nolan used for his adaptation.

segments.title: The Homeric question and whether Homer existed
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether Homer was a real person or a group, the lack of outside historical references, and the suggestion that he was from Ionia and possibly the blind bard Demodocus.

segments.title: Introduction to the main themes
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the Odyssey's central concepts of xenia (hospitality) and nostos (homecoming) before breaking.

segments.title: Xenia: rules of guest and host
segments.summary: Xenia is described as a set of divine rules under Zeus governing how hosts treat strangers and guests, including food, wine, baths, and protection.

segments.title: Nostos and the theme of homecoming
segments.summary: Nostos, or homecoming, is described as the core of the Odyssey, reflecting Greek seafaring life and long separations from family.

segments.title: Off-topic chat about reading Moby Dick
segments.summary: Josh mentions he has started reading Moby Dick alongside a podcast recap, and the hosts briefly chat about it.

segments.title: Break before the plot summary
segments.summary: The hosts tease the plot summary of books in the Odyssey and take a break.

segments.title: Return and spoiler warning
segments.summary: Josh returns and warns that the plot summary contains spoilers and will identify film actors and their roles.

segments.title: Cast of the Nolan film and the Trojan War setup
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the film's casting of Matt Damon as Odysseus, and the premise that the Trojan War began when Paris took Helen and lasted ten years, leaving Odysseus gone for twenty years. They also mention Lupita Nyong'o as Helen and Elon Musk's criticism of the casting.

segments.title: Penelope, Telemachus and the suitors
segments.summary: Josh describes the family in the film: Penelope played by Anne Hathaway, Telemachus by Tom Holland, and Robert Pattinson as the villainous suitor Antinous. The suitors take over the palace.

segments.title: Suitors and Penelope's weaving trick
segments.summary: The hosts describe the suitors pressing Penelope to choose a new husband and her delay tactic of weaving and unweaving a funeral shroud for Odysseus's father Laertes.

segments.title: Banter about Odysseus's father's name
segments.summary: A joking exchange about the name of Odysseus's father, with the hosts teasing each other.

segments.title: Athena sends Telemachus to find his father
segments.summary: Athena urges Telemachus to search for his father. Zendaya plays Athena, and Telemachus visits King Menelaus in Sparta, who says Odysseus is alive and held on Calypso's island. Benny Safdie plays Agamemnon and John Bernthal plays Menelaus.

segments.title: Calypso and the flashback structure
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the Odyssey is nonlinear and that the story is partly a flashback. Calypso holds Odysseus for about seven years until Athena persuades Zeus to release him. Charlize Theron plays Calypso.

segments.title: Poseidon wrecks Odysseus's raft
segments.summary: Odysseus leaves on a raft but Poseidon wrecks it as punishment for the blinding of his son the Cyclops. He is shipwrecked and taken in by the Phaeacians.

segments.title: Odysseus recounts his story to the Phaeacians
segments.summary: The Phaeacian king asks Odysseus to tell his story at a feast, which becomes the main flashback of the poem.

segments.title: Departure from Troy and Athena's storms
segments.summary: After leaving with about 600 soldiers, Athena sends storms because of war crimes committed at Troy, and the fleet lands among the lotus eaters.

segments.title: Lotus eaters and the Cyclops
segments.summary: The crew eats lotus and wants to stay; Odysseus drags them back to the ships. Next they reach the island of the Cyclops, where Polyphemus eats the men until Odysseus blinds him.

segments.title: Polyphemus, the puppet and the Laestrygonians
segments.summary: Josh and the host discuss the Cyclops puppet in the film and the Laestrygonians, a tribe of giant cannibals. The host says Polyphemus was wronged first, per their reading, though Josh has not verified it.

segments.title: Poseidon's curse and the island of Circe
segments.summary: Polyphemus prays to Poseidon, who wrecks the fleet. The survivors reach Circe's island, where she turns the men into pigs until Odysseus forces them back.

segments.title: Circe's island and the underworld
segments.summary: Circe is an enchantress who falls for Odysseus. The hosts describe his trip to the underworld where he meets Agamemnon, his mother, and the prophet Tiresias, who warns him not to eat Helios's sacred cattle.

segments.title: Circe's advice: beeswax and Scylla
segments.summary: Before continuing to Ithaca, Circe gives Odysseus beeswax for his men's ears and advises steering toward Scylla rather than Charybdis, plus a repeated warning about the cattle.

segments.title: The Sirens
segments.summary: Odysseus has his men plug their ears with beeswax and tie him to the mast so he can hear the Sirens' song without being able to steer toward them. It works.

segments.title: Scylla and Charybdis
segments.summary: The fleet navigates the strait between Scylla, a six-headed monster, and Charybdis, a whirlpool. Odysseus chooses Scylla, losing about six men, and the hosts describe the 'between a rock and a hard place' origin.

segments.title: Helios, the sacred cattle and the shipwreck
segments.summary: The men eat Helios's sacred cattle despite warnings. Zeus destroys the ship as it departs, leaving Odysseus alone, and he washes ashore at Calypso's island, ending the flashback.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts announce a break before returning to wrap up the Odyssey.

segments.title: Odysseus's homecoming in disguise
segments.summary: In books 12 onward, Odysseus reaches Ithaca and disguises himself as a beggar. Only his old dog and nurse, played by John Leguizamo, recognize him. Telemachus reveals himself to his father.

segments.title: The bow contest and the marriage bed
segments.summary: Penelope holds a contest where suitors must string Odysseus's bow and shoot through twelve axe heads. Only the disguised Odysseus succeeds. Penelope tests him with the olive-tree marriage bed.

segments.title: Battle with suitors and Athena's peace
segments.summary: Odysseus and Telemachus defeat the suitors. Families of the suitors then start a civil war until Athena steps in and stops it.

segments.title: Historical evidence for Troy
segments.summary: The hosts describe Hisarlik in Turkey, the site excavated by Heinrich Schliemann, with layers showing repeated burning. Layer seven is linked to Homer's era, and slingshot stones are cited as evidence of war.

segments.title: Trojan horse, sea routes and allegorical monsters
segments.summary: Some pre-Odyssey finds show men emerging from a wheeled horse, though it may be symbolic. The monsters may represent navigational hazards, like Scylla and Charybdis in the Strait of Messina, and Mount Etna has been proposed as the Cyclops.
topics: Scylla and Charybdis Strait of Messina

segments.title: Why the Odyssey endures
segments.summary: The hosts argue the story's universal themes of homecoming, adventure, regret, family and good versus bad guys keep it relevant, and its values still make sense today.

segments.title: Adaptations: Joyce, Atwood and O Brother, Where Art Thou?
segments.summary: The hosts list adaptations: James Joyce's Ulysses, Margaret Atwood's The Penelopiad, and the Coen brothers' O Brother, Where Art Thou?, which parallels the poem with George Clooney as Ulysses and other characters.
topics: O Brother Where Art Thou Coen brothers

segments.title: Telegony, the lost sequel
segments.summary: The hosts describe the lost sequel Telegony, attributed to Eugamon of Cyrene, in which Telegonus kills Odysseus. It is known only from references in other writings.

segments.title: Listener mail: rope and pulleys
segments.summary: Jonathan writes in praising the rope episode and suggesting that rope and pulleys enabled building temples, walls, aqueducts and bridges.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank Jonathan, promote listener emails and sign off with production credits.
